CHAPTER 4 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4 · LEARNING AREA 4 · APRIL · MAY

Prisms

A chocolate box with a triangular cross-section, a pencil with six edges, a tent, a honeycomb: all of these are prisms. You learn to recognise them, to draw them as an oblique drawing and to unfold them into a net. Then you calculate how much card you need for a package and how much fits inside. At the end there is a project: how much packaging waste can be saved?

12 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise prisms by their properties and build models
  • draw prisms as an oblique drawing (cabinet projection)
  • draw nets of solids and calculate the surface area
  • calculate the volume of right prisms and composite solids
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

What is the volume of a cuboid measuring 5 cm, 4 cm and 3 cm?

$5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 60$ cm³

How many faces does a cube have?

Six squares.

A right-angled triangle has the arms 3 cm and 4 cm. What is its area?

$\tfrac12 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 6$ cm²

How many cm³ are 1 litre?

$1\,\ell = 1\,\text{dm}^3 = 1000\,\text{cm}^3$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Prisms and oblique drawings

The chocolate box has a triangle at the front and at the back, with three rectangles in between. If you push the triangle straight backwards, you get exactly this solid. That is how every prism is made: a polygon is moved at right angles to itself.

A right prism has two congruent, parallel polygons as its base and top. The other faces are rectangles and together form the lateral surface. The distance between the base and the top is the height $h$ of the prism. Cuboids and cubes are special prisms.

In an oblique drawing in cabinet projection you draw the front face in its true size. The edges that run backwards are drawn at $45^\circ$ and half as long. Hidden edges are dashed.

KEY POINT · PRISMS

Right prism: base and top congruent and parallel, side faces rectangles, height $h$.

A prism with an $n$-gon as its base has $n + 2$ faces, $2n$ vertices and $3n$ edges.

Cabinet projection: front face in true size, backwards at $45^\circ$ and $\tfrac12$ as long, hidden edges dashed.

Not a prism: pyramid (comes to a point), sphere, cone. A cylinder is almost a prism, but its base is not a polygon.

On squared paper: “half as long at $45^\circ$” means: for 2 cm of depth draw 1 cm at a slant. The diagonal of one square is only about 0.7 cm, so measure with the set square.

INTERACTIVE · PRISMS AS OBLIQUE DRAWINGS

Choose a base and change the size. Which edges become dashed?

EXAMPLE 1 · VERTICES, EDGES, FACES

A pencil is a hexagonal prism. How many faces, vertices and edges does it have (without the tip)?

Base a hexagon, $n = 6$: faces $6 + 2$, vertices $2 \cdot 6$, edges $3 \cdot 6$.

8 faces, 12 vertices, 18 edges

EXAMPLE 2 · AN OBLIQUE DRAWING

Draw a cuboid 4 cm wide, 2 cm high and 6 cm deep as an oblique drawing.

At the front a rectangle 4 cm by 2 cm. From each corner an edge at $45^\circ$, but only 3 cm long (half the depth). Join the ends.

The three edges at the bottom left back corner are hidden.

EXERCISES

Prism or not? a) shoebox b) carton with a triangular cross-section c) football d) building block with an L-shaped front e) ice-cream cone

a) yes, cuboid   b) yes, triangular prism   c) no   d) yes, the L-shape is the base   e) no, a cone

Fill in the table: base triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, octagon → number of faces, vertices, edges.

Triangle: 5, 6, 9 · quadrilateral: 6, 8, 12 · pentagon: 7, 10, 15 · octagon: 10, 16, 24

Make an oblique drawing of a triangular prism: the front face is a right-angled triangle with the arms 4 cm and 3 cm, the prism is 6 cm deep.

At the front the triangle in true size. From the corners 3 cm backwards at $45^\circ$. The edges behind the solid dashed. Compare with the widget (triangular prism, $a = 4$, $h = 6$).

Build a prism with a pentagonal base from drinking straws and modelling clay. How many straws and how many balls of clay do you need?

Edges: $3 \cdot 5 = 15$ straws. Vertices: $2 \cdot 5 = 10$ balls of clay.

A prism has 30 edges. What is its base? How many vertices and faces does it have?

$3n = 30$, so $n = 10$: a decagon. 20 vertices, 12 faces. Check with Euler’s formula: $20 + 12 - 30 = 2$ ✓

TEST YOURSELF!

How many edges does a hexagonal prism have?

$3 \cdot 6$

How many faces does a pentagonal prism have?

$5 + 2$

A cuboid is 6 cm deep. How long do you draw the depth in the oblique drawing?

Half as long: 3 cm.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Net and surface area

The chocolate box, cut open, lies flat: two triangles and a long strip of three rectangles. The strip is as high as the box is long, and as wide as the perimeter of the triangle. All the card together is the surface area.

A net of a solid is made when you cut the surface of the solid open along edges and spread it out flat. For a prism it consists of two bases and the lateral surface. The lateral surface is a rectangle: as wide as the perimeter $u$ of the base, as high as the prism.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA

Lateral area: $M = u \cdot h$ ($u$ is the perimeter of the base)

Surface area: $O = 2 \cdot G + M$

For a cuboid with $a$, $b$, $c$: $O = 2ab + 2ac + 2bc$

Many nets: a cube has 11 different nets. But not every arrangement of six squares can be folded into a cube.

Glue flaps are not part of the surface. For a model you add them to the drawing.

INTERACTIVE · THE NET

At the top and bottom the bases $G$, in between the lateral surface $M$. Switch to the oblique drawing and back.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE CHOCOLATE BOX

The box has an equilateral triangle with 4 cm sides and a height of $3.5$ cm as its base, and it is 20 cm long. How much card do you need?

$G = \tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 3.5 = 7$ cm². $u = 12$ cm, $M = 12 \cdot 20 = 240$ cm².

$O = 2 \cdot 7 + 240 =$ 254 cm²

EXAMPLE 4 · A TENT

A tent is a triangular prism: at the front a triangle 2 m wide and $1.5$ m high, the sides of the roof are $1.8$ m wide each, the tent is 3 m long. How much fabric do you need, including the groundsheet?

$G = \tfrac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 1.5 = 1.5$ m². $u = 2 + 1.8 + 1.8 = 5.6$ m, $M = 5.6 \cdot 3 = 16.8$ m².

$O = 3 + 16.8 =$ $19.8$ m²

EXERCISES

Calculate the surface area: a) cube with an edge length of 5 cm   b) cuboid 8 cm, 5 cm, 2 cm   c) triangular prism, base right-angled with 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm, height 10 cm

a) $6 \cdot 25 = 150$ cm²   b) $2 \cdot 40 + 2 \cdot 16 + 2 \cdot 10 = 132$ cm²   c) $G = 6$, $M = 12 \cdot 10 = 120$, $O = 132$ cm²

Draw two different nets of a cuboid measuring 3 cm, 2 cm and 1 cm. Check by cutting out and folding.

For example: four side faces next to each other as a strip, with the two small faces attached at the top and bottom. Or a “cross”. Important: opposite faces must not lie next to each other in the net.

A pencil is a hexagonal prism, 17 cm long. The hexagon has 4 mm sides and an area of $41.6$ mm². How big is the painted lateral surface in cm²?

$u = 6 \cdot 4 = 24$ mm, $h = 170$ mm, $M = 24 \cdot 170 = 4080$ mm² $= 40.8$ cm².

Which arrangements of six squares are nets of a cube? Draw three correct ones and one wrong one.

Correct, for example: cross (4 in a row, one each above and below the second square), “staircase” (2–2–2 staggered), 1–4–1 in another position. Wrong: 6 in a row, or a 2 × 3 rectangle.

A cube and a cuboid have the same volume of 64 cm³. The cuboid is 16 cm long, 2 cm wide, 2 cm high. Which needs more packaging?

Cube: edge 4 cm, $O = 6 \cdot 16 = 96$ cm². Cuboid: $2 \cdot 32 + 2 \cdot 32 + 2 \cdot 4 = 136$ cm². The long cuboid needs a lot more.

TEST YOURSELF!

Surface area of a cube with a 5 cm edge?

$6 \cdot 25$

Surface area of a cuboid measuring 8 cm, 5 cm, 2 cm?

$80 + 32 + 20$

Chocolate box: $G = 7$ cm², $u = 12$ cm, $h = 20$ cm. Surface area?

$14 + 240$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Volume and composite solids

For a cuboid you first lay one layer of cubes on the bottom: as many as the area of the base. Then you stack as many layers as the cuboid is high. This works for every prism: each layer is as big as the base.

So the volume of a prism is base times height. For a composite solid you split it into prisms and add, or you fill it in to make one large prism and subtract, just as with areas.

KEY POINT · VOLUME

Prism: $V = G \cdot h$   ·   Cuboid: $V = a \cdot b \cdot c$   ·   Cube: $V = a^3$

$1\,\text{dm}^3 = 1000\,\text{cm}^3 = 1\,\ell$   ·   $1\,\text{cm}^3 = 1\,\text{m}\ell$   ·   $1\,\text{m}^3 = 1000\,\ell$

Careful with the height: the height of the prism is the distance between the base and the top. For a prism lying down that is its length.

The principle of reduction again: you work out the base with the formulas from chapter 3.3.

INTERACTIVE · SURFACE AREA AND VOLUME

Double the height. What happens to the volume, and what to the surface area? Then double the base edge.

EXAMPLE 5 · A DYKE

The dyke from chapter 3.3 has a trapezium cross-section of 18 m². It is 500 m long. How much earth is in it?

The dyke is a trapezium prism lying down: $V = G \cdot h = 18 \cdot 500$.

9000 m³

EXAMPLE 6 · COMPOSITE

A house consists of a cuboid (10 m long, 8 m wide, 6 m high) and a gable roof (triangular prism, gable 8 m wide and 4 m high). What is the enclosed volume?

Cuboid: $10 \cdot 8 \cdot 6 = 480$ m³. Roof: $G = \tfrac12 \cdot 8 \cdot 4 = 16$ m², $V = 16 \cdot 10 = 160$ m³.

640 m³

PROJECT · PACKAGING WASTE

🌍 Every package costs material, and most of it ends up as rubbish. Investigate in groups:

  • Collect five packages with similar contents. Measure them and calculate the volume and the surface area.
  • Work out for each: how many cm² of card do you need per 100 cm³ of contents?
  • Design a package for the same contents that needs less material. Build a model.
  • Present your results: what can manufacturers and customers do?

Alternative: we build a fantasy city out of prisms and calculate the volume each building encloses.

EXERCISES

Calculate the volume: a) cuboid 6 cm, 4 cm, 2.5 cm   b) triangular prism with $G = 12$ cm² and $h = 8$ cm   c) trapezium prism with $a = 5$ cm, $c = 3$ cm, height of the trapezium 2 cm, height of the prism 10 cm

a) 60 cm³   b) 96 cm³   c) $G = 8$ cm², $V = 80$ cm³

An aquarium is 80 cm long, 40 cm wide and 50 cm high. How many litres fit inside if it is filled to 5 cm below the rim?

$80 \cdot 40 \cdot 45 = 144\,000$ cm³ $= 144$ ℓ

A concrete staircase has three steps. Each step is 20 cm high and 30 cm deep, the staircase is 1 m wide. Calculate the volume. Tip: the side view is the base.

Side view: $30 \cdot 20 + 60 \cdot 20 + 90 \cdot 20 = 3600$ cm². $V = 3600 \cdot 100 = 360\,000$ cm³ $= 0.36$ m³.

A juice carton holds 1 litre. Its base is 7 cm by 6 cm. At least how high must it be?

$1000 : 42 \approx 23.8$ cm

If you double all the edges of a cube, how do the surface area and the volume change? Try it in the widget with the cuboid.

Surface area: four times as much ($2 \cdot 2$). Volume: eight times as much ($2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2$).

TEST YOURSELF!

Aquarium 80 cm by 40 cm, water 45 cm deep. How many litres?

$144\,000$ cm³

House: cuboid 480 m³ and roof 160 m³. Enclosed volume?

$480 + 160$

All the edges of a cube are doubled. How many times the old volume is the new volume?

$2^3 = 8$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Convert: a) $2.5$ ℓ to cm³   b) 750 cm³ to ℓ   c) $1.2$ m³ to ℓ

a) 2500 cm³   b) $0.75$ ℓ   c) 1200 ℓ

Connecting with chapter 2.2: a cuboid has a base of 20 cm². Make a table height → volume. What kind of assignment is this? And with a fixed volume of 120 cm³: base → height?

Height → volume: directly proportional ($V = 20 \cdot h$). Base → height with a fixed volume: inversely proportional ($G \cdot h = 120$).

Connecting with chapter 1.2: a cube has an edge length of $\tfrac34$ m. Calculate the volume and the surface area as fractions.

$V = \left(\tfrac34\right)^3 = \tfrac{27}{64}$ m³. $O = 6 \cdot \tfrac{9}{16} = \tfrac{27}{8} = 3\tfrac38$ m².

A square hole of 2 cm by 2 cm is drilled through the middle of a wooden cube with 6 cm edges, from front to back. What is the remaining volume? How does the surface area change?

$V = 216 - 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6 = 192$ cm³. Surface area: 4 cm² each are missing at the front and back, inside 4 walls of $2 \cdot 6 = 12$ cm² each are added. $O = 216 - 8 + 48 = 256$ cm², so more than before.

EXCURSIONNATURE AND MATHEMATICS

The honeycomb

🐝 Bees build their combs from small hexagonal prisms. Why hexagons of all things? Wax is like packaging: every wall costs material. As early as 36 BC the Roman scholar Varro suspected that hexagons are the most economical solution.

The mathematical question is: how do you divide a plane into cells of equal size so that the walls together are as short as possible? Squares and triangles also fill the plane without gaps, but regular hexagons need less wall. That there really is no better division was only proved in 1999 by the American mathematician Thomas Hales. So the conjecture was more than 2000 years old.

Check it: a square and a regular hexagon both have an area of about 10 cm². The square has sides of about 3.16 cm, the hexagon of about 1.96 cm. Which has the smaller perimeter?

Square: $4 \cdot 3.16 \approx 12.6$ cm. Hexagon: $6 \cdot 1.96 \approx 11.8$ cm. The hexagon needs less wall.

Sources: Thomas C. Hales, “The Honeycomb Conjecture”, Discrete & Computational Geometry 25 (2001), pp. 1–22 (preprint 1999). The conjecture is traced back to Marcus Terentius Varro (36 BC).
